everyday-actions-01.semantic_alignment: Indonesian kirim and Malaysian hantar both cover sending an item. Malaysian kirim is also used for this sense, so a distinct everyday preference for hantar is unresolved.

claims.proposition: The proposed terms share the sending sense, but the supplied usage does not settle whether hantar is preferred over kirim for the same everyday context in Malaysia.

everyday-actions-02.semantic_alignment: Indonesian cuci and Malaysian basuh share this sense. Malaysian cuci can be equally natural for particular objects, making the broad everyday preference disputed.

claims.proposition: The proposed words both describe washing, but object-dependent Malaysian use of cuci prevents a general preference claim for basuh.

everyday-actions-03.semantic_alignment: Indonesian lempar and Malaysian baling both fit a physical throw of a ball; baling may suggest a forceful throw.

claims.proposition: Lempar and baling are natural locale choices for throwing a ball by hand, though baling can carry a stronger force nuance.

everyday-actions-04.semantic_alignment: Indonesian dorong and Malaysian tolak both describe moving an object away by applying force.

claims.proposition: Dorong and tolak are natural locale choices for physically pushing an object away.

everyday-actions-05.semantic_alignment: The intended actions are expressed clearly by Indonesian menyetir and Malaysian memandu. The proposed bare forms setir and pandu do not reliably serve as neutral standalone verbs for this sense.

claims.proposition: The proposed setir–pandu pair is unsuitable as a neutral verb pair: setir is commonly a steering-wheel noun, while memandu is the ordinary Malaysian verb for driving a car.

everyday-actions-06.semantic_alignment: Indonesian bicara fits the sense. Malaysian cakap belongs to the right word family, but bercakap is the clearer neutral verb for talking to someone.

claims.proposition: The proposed bicara–cakap pair has a form and register mismatch for a neutral verb card because bercakap is the straightforward Malaysian verb form.

everyday-actions-07.semantic_alignment: Indonesian coba and Malaysian cuba are recognizably related everyday forms that both express trying an action.

claims.proposition: Coba and cuba are commonly used for trying an action and differ in spelling while retaining the same everyday sense.
